identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE sometimes produces fewer total extractions than prior systems because prior systems output many redundant extractions; when redundancy is discounted, MinIE is competitive in extraction counts.
evidence: Discussion and Table 3: total and non-redundant counts reported; authors explain many prior-system variants are redundant (Stanford OIE noted).
uncertainty_flags: Redundancy definition is operational (subsequence within same sentence) and may bias comparisons; alternate redundancy metrics may change conclusions.
The effect depends on how ClausIE generates multiple extractions and on postprocessing; may differ with other base extractors.

identified_claims.claim_text: Main sources of MinIE errors are dependency parsing errors and NER mistakes; collocation/mode errors arise when dictionaries miss true collocations leading to over-minimization.
evidence: Sec. 7.4: qualitative error analysis linking parser/NER errors and missing collocations in D to MinIE mistakes.
uncertainty_flags: No quantitative breakdown of error contributions is provided to quantify the relative importance of each source.
Dependency on a particular parser/NER version (Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1) means error rates are tied to those specific choices.

identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE is implemented on top of ClausIE because ClausIE separates identification of constituents from proposition generation, detects clause types, and is state-of-the-art, enabling MinIE's rewriting pipeline.
evidence: Sec. 3: rationale for building on ClausIE; Sec. 4: descriptions of enriching ClausIE output prior to minimization.
uncertainty_flags: Claim about portability to other OIE systems is made but not empirically validated; practicality of integrating MinIE into other pipelines is not demonstrated.

strengths.title: Clear conceptual framing: minimization + annotations
strengths.description: The paper articulates a coherent conceptual frame: minimize surface triples while externalizing removed semantics via annotations (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities), enabling shorter, more canonical extractions without losing representational content.
evidence: Introduction: explicit framing; Sec. 5: detailed annotation procedures; Table 1: illustrative example where MinIE records polarity/attribution.

strengths.title: Practical, implemented system with modes
strengths.description: MinIE is implemented on a real OIE pipeline (ClausIE) and exposes multiple, well-described modes (safe/frequency/collocations/aggressive) allowing practitioners to select trade-offs for different uses.
evidence: Sec. 3 overview and Sec. 6 modes: operational descriptions; experimental study using MinIE-S/F/C/A.

strengths.title: Empirical evaluation across multiple datasets
strengths.description: Authors evaluate MinIE on a large unlabeled corpus (NYT-10k) for extraction statistics and on two labeled 200-sentence sets (NYT, Wiki) for precision/attribution metrics, enabling multi-faceted comparisons with prior systems.
evidence: Sec. 7.1 dataset description and Sec. 7.2/7.3 results in Tables 3 and 4.

strengths.title: Annotation types that address a practical gap
strengths.description: Adding polarity, modality, and quantity annotations (and attaching factuality to attributions) addresses an acknowledged limitation in OIE outputs relevant to downstream reasoning (absence of negative evidence, modality ambiguity).
evidence: Introduction discussion on negative evidence; Sec. 5.1-5.4 detailing how these annotations are produced and used.

concerns.title: Limited coverage of factuality and attribution detectors
concerns.description: Negation, modality, and attribution are detected using small lexicons and simple patterns (negation lexicon {no, not, never, none}; modality lexicon from Saurí & Pustejovsky/WordNet; attribution dictionary), which capture only 'easy cases' and omit complex scope, embedded negation, and nuanced attributions.
evidence: Sec. 5.1: small negation lexicon; Sec. 5.2: lexicon-based modality; Sec. 5.3: attribution from clause patterns and a dictionary; authors explicitly say they handle only easy cases and do not address negation scope/double negation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide an error-sampled quantitative analysis showing how often these detectors fire and where they fail (e.g., confusion matrix on annotated factuality/attribution cases). Consider integrating more advanced factuality scopes (e.g., full scope resolution) or clarifying limitations in the annotation semantics in the README and labeling guidelines.

concerns.title: Evaluation sample size and statistical reporting
concerns.description: Labeled precision estimates are based on small samples (NYT n=200, Wiki n=200); the paper lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics, confidence intervals, or significance testing to support claims of competitive precision.
evidence: Sec. 7.1: labeling described for 200-sentence samples; Sec. 7.3: precision claims without reported confidence intervals or agreement statistics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa / Krippendorff's alpha), provide exact raw counts per system and confidence intervals for precision metrics; increase labeled sample size or apply bootstrapping to better estimate variance.

concerns.title: Operational redundancy definition influences recall comparisons
concerns.description: The redundancy definition (a triple t1 redundant if it is a subsequence of another triple from the same sentence) is arbitrary and may bias recall comparisons (favoring systems that produce fewer variants), affecting reported competitiveness on extraction counts.
evidence: Sec. 7.1 measures: redundancy defined as subsequence; Sec. 7.2 discussion: Stanford OIE produces many (short) redundant variants and counts differ substantially when redundancy discounted.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide alternative redundancy measures (e.g., normalized canonical forms, semantic equivalence clusters, or a human-judged redundancy sample) and show sensitivity of non-redundant counts to the redundancy definition.

concerns.title: Risk of overfitting when building dictionary D from same corpus
concerns.description: MinIE-F constructs dictionary D from frequent constituents in the NYT corpus; training D on the same corpus used in evaluation can inflate the apparent success of corpus-frequency-driven minimization, limiting generalization claims.
evidence: Sec. 7.1: MinIE-F built dictionary using entire NYT corpus; Sec. 6.2: frequency mode uses corpus frequency threshold (example ≥10).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report cross-corpus experiments: run MinIE-F with a D built on a different corpus (or away from the evaluation split) and measure performance shifts; clarify in text that MinIE-F is domain-adaptive and requires corpus-suitable D.

concerns.title: Proxy metric for minimality may not reflect semantic adequacy
concerns.description: Using mean word count and standard deviation as a proxy for minimality conflates brevity with semantic preservation; shorter extractions could lose essential context even if they are shorter.
evidence: Sec. 7.1: authors state mean word count is used as proxy for minimality; Sec. 7.2: results rely on µ±σ comparisons.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include human judgments or downstream-task evaluations (e.g., QA or KB population accuracy) to measure semantic adequacy of minimized extractions; add precision/recall conditioned on annotations being used vs ignored.

concerns.title: Portability claim to other OIE systems not empirically validated
concerns.description: Although authors claim MinIE techniques can be integrated into other OIE systems, experiments are performed only on ClausIE outputs; thus portability and interaction effects with other extractors are untested.
evidence: Sec. 3: authors state techniques can be integrated into any OIE system but implement on top of ClausIE only.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either temper portability claims or demonstrate a small-scale porting experiment onto another extractor (e.g., Stanford OIE pipeline) and report differences.

comparable_works.relevance: Base system used by MinIE; provides clause identification and extraction pipeline that MinIE augments.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE builds directly on ClausIE's clause structure but adds enrichment, basic minimization, annotations, and modes for further lexical minimization.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript Sec. 3 and Sec. 4 describe building MinIE on ClausIE; references include Del Corro and Gemulla (2013).

comparable_works.relevance: A recent OIE system that also uses aggressive minimization; used as a comparative baseline.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both perform minimization; Stanford OIE deletes subconstituents by dependency types and frequency constraints; MinIE differs by producing factual annotations and richer, mode-driven minimizations.
comparable_works.source_trace: Related work Sec. 2 and experimental comparisons Sec. 7.2/7.3 reference Angeli et al. (2015).

comparable_works.relevance: Introduced annotated OIE extractions (attribution and clause modifiers); MinIE extends annotation scope.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: OLLIE uses attribution and clause-modifier annotations; MinIE extends annotations to polarity/modality/quantities and integrates minimization modes.
comparable_works.source_trace: Introduction and Related work discuss OLLIE and its annotation types.

comparable_works.relevance: Proposed frequency-based lexical constraints to avoid overly-specific relations; conceptually related to MinIE-F's frequency dictionary.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE-F generalizes the idea to subjects/arguments and uses more structured dependency-driven minimization and annotations.
comparable_works.source_trace: Related work Sec. 2 discusses ReVerb and inspirations for frequency-based constraints.

comparable_works.relevance: Provides factuality representation (polarity and modality) used as the conceptual basis for MinIE's factuality annotations.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE adopts a simplified CT/PS polarity scheme from Saurí & Pustejovsky but implements only lexicon/rule detectors (easy cases) rather than their full approach.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 5 references Saurí and Pustejovsky (2012) as basis for factuality annotation.

uncertainty_flags: Factuality/modality/polarity detectors are lexicon/rule-based and limited to easy cases; scope and coverage remain uncertain.
Evaluation labeled sets are small (200 sentences each) and inter-annotator agreement/confidence intervals are not reported.
MinIE-F uses a dictionary built from the same NYT corpus; risk of overfitting and domain dependence.
Dependency on a particular parser/NER (Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1) ties results to upstream tool performance; portability to other parsers is untested.
alternative_interpretations: Shorter mean extraction length could be an artifact of deduplication logic, aggressive canonicalization, or different clause-enrichment choices rather than strictly better minimality.
Precision gains of MinIE-S/F/C might partly stem from removing error-prone modifiers that previously caused ClausIE failures rather than truly preserving more correct semantics.

The relatively good precision of MinIE modes could partly be due to domain overlap between the frequency-dictionary training corpus and the evaluation corpus (NYT), i.e., corpus-specific optimization.
Annotations exist but downstream systems may ignore them; hence, improvements in triple brevity do not automatically imply improved downstream task performance.
transparency_notes: Request release of dictionary D contents (WordNet/Wiktionary subsets and corpus-derived lists), full MinIE code, and exact parser/NER configurations to reproduce minimization decisions.
Provide labeling guidelines and raw annotated labels and annotator IDs to allow auditors to assess inter-annotator agreement and label ambiguity.
Report exact numeric tables for all precision/recall/length numbers (not just summarized parentheses), and provide statistical tests or confidence intervals.
Clarify the exact frequency thresholds and corpus splits used to build MinIE-F's dictionary and whether evaluation data were excluded from dictionary construction.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The idea of minimizing surface triples and externalizing removed semantics via structured annotations departs from typical OIE outputs and lacks a close precedent; this is an innovation signal but does not by itself guarantee correctness, robustness, or utility for downstream tasks.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: Upstream parsers and NER achieve sufficiently high accuracy so that stable subconstituents and dependency-driven minimizations are reliable.
Downstream consumers of OIE outputs are annotation-aware and use polarity/modality/attribution/quantity annotations when performing inference or KB population.
Dictionary D is constructed to cover domain-specific collocations or is learned robustly from diverse corpora to avoid over-minimization of essential collocations.
Factuality detectors are extended (or replaced) with higher-coverage scope-aware models or classifiers to capture complex negation/modality/attribution phenomena.

novelty_lenses.rationale: MinIE reframes OIE output design: instead of treating every extraction as a fixed surface triple, it proposes a canonicalization process that factors out factuality and modifiers into structured annotations, enabling shorter canonical facts. This conceptual move—minimize surface facts while retaining semantics in annotations—is not a small incremental tweak but a potentially transformative representation change for downstream reasoning.
evidence: Paper claims explicit removal of negation/modality/attribution/quantities into annotations and positions this as addressing absence of negative evidence in KB/population methods (Introduction, Sec. 5).
Comparison to OLLIE (which had limited annotations) shows MinIE expands annotation types.
uncertainty_flags: Implementation-level simplifications (small lexicons, dependency heuristics) limit immediate robustness; novelty as representation is distinct from validated utility.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Partly incremental relative to prior OIE annotation/minimization work
novelty_lenses.rationale: MinIE combines several previously explored ideas—relation enrichment (Fader et al.), annotations (OLLIE), and frequency/collocation constraints (ReVerb)—and packages them into a practical pipeline with mode controls. From this perspective, many components are existing techniques integrated and operationalized rather than wholly new algorithmic advances.
evidence: Related work explicitly positions MinIE as building on ClausIE, OLLIE, ReVerb, and Stanford OIE, and the techniques (lexicons, dictionaries, dependency-based drops) are established.
Evaluation compares against those systems and shows empirical improvements, but improvements hinge on engineering choices (dictionaries, modes).
uncertainty_flags: The integrative packaging and explicit annotation of factuality types remain distinctive; hybrid view of disruption + incremental engineering applies.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident (lower bound) in the system-level factual statements (MinIE's implementation and that it shortens extractions) because these are well-documented and supported by experiments. I am less confident (upper bound) about claims of generalization, robustness of factuality detectors, and downstream utility due to limited labeled sample sizes, rule-based detectors for complex phenomena, and corpus-dependent dictionary construction; hence the interval reflects a mix of strong evidence for the core idea but uncertainty for broad applicability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents MinIE, a rewriting layer built on ClausIE that (a) enriches ClausIE relations, (b) performs basic minimization by removing polarity, modality, attribution, and quantity signals and converting them to annotations, and (c) applies controlled minimization modes (safe, frequency, collocations, aggressive) to drop additional surface material while recording removed content. The authors evaluate extraction-length statistics on a large unlabeled NYT-10k sample and factual/attribution precision on two labeled 200-sentence samples (NYT, Wiki), comparing to ClausIE, OLLIE, and Stanford OIE. Evidence in the manuscript supports that MinIE shortens extractions (mean token length falls monotonically with aggressiveness) and that safe/intermediate modes maintain competitive factual and attribution precision on the provided small labeled samples. Key weaknesses are dependence on lexicon/rule-based factuality detectors limited to 'easy cases', reliance on a single upstream pipeline (ClausIE + Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1), underspecified construction of dictionary D (domain sensitivity), small labeled samples with no reported statistical uncertainty or IAA, and conflation of word-count minimality with preserved informativeness. I flag uncertainty where claims rest on these operational choices and suggest concrete audits (detector-level evaluation, parser/NER sensitivity, and downstream task evaluation) to strengthen validity.
logical_argument_graph: OIE extractions are often overly-specific and contain embedded polarity/modality/attribution/quantities which hinder downstream reasoning.
MinIE rewrites ClausIE extractions by enriching relations then performing basic minimization that removes polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities and records them as annotations.
MinIE provides multiple modes (S, F, C, A) that vary aggressiveness by defining stable subconstituents using NER, dependency structure, and dictionary D.
On NYT-10k, MinIE modes reduce mean extraction length versus ClausIE; aggressiveness correlates with shorter output.
On labeled NYT/Wiki samples (n≈200 each), MinIE-S/F/C maintain higher or competitive factual precision compared to baselines; MinIE-A is shorter but loses some precision.
Main error sources identified are dependency parser and NER mistakes and dictionary coverage problems.
Therefore, minimized annotated triples can be more compact while often preserving factual correctness, offering a practical precision/minimality trade-off.

identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE produces minimized, annotated OIE extractions by identifying and removing overly-specific parts of extractions and representing polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities as separate annotations instead of embedding them in the surface triple.
evidence: Abstract and Introduction explicitly state MinIE removes parts considered overly specific and represents polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities with annotations.
Sec. 5 subsections describe detection and removal for polarity (5.1), modality (5.2), attribution (5.3), and quantities (5.4) and creation of annotations.
uncertainty_flags: Detection methods are rule/lexicon-based and limited to 'easy cases', so annotations may miss complex phenomena (e.g., negation scope, nested modality).
The manuscript describes the design and implementation but does not provide detector-level recall/precision for these annotations.

identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE provides multiple minimization modes (MinIE-S, MinIE-F, MinIE-C, MinIE-A) that trade off minimality and precision: safe mode performs conservative drops, frequency and collocations modes use dictionaries to drop additional modifiers, and aggressive mode drops most uncertain words.
evidence: Sec. 3 overview and detailed Sec. 6 describe the four modes and their rules/resources.
Sec. 6.2 explains the role of dictionary D and how MinIE-F and MinIE-C differ.
uncertainty_flags: Operational thresholds (e.g., frequency ≥10) and dictionary contents are only summarized; sensitivity to those choices is not tested.
Mode effectiveness depends on NER and dependency parse quality and on D’s domain coverage.

identified_claims.claim_text: Across multiple datasets, all MinIE modes produce extractions that are substantially shorter on average (mean word length) than those of the underlying ClausIE and many prior systems; more aggressive modes produce shorter extractions.
evidence: NYT-10k Table 3: ClausIE mean 10.9±7 vs MinIE-S 7.2±4.2 ... MinIE-A 4.7±1.9; authors report statistically smaller lengths than ClausIE and monotonic decrease with aggressiveness.
uncertainty_flags: Minimality is proxied by mean token count; shorter length does not necessarily imply preserved informativeness.
Results are reported for specific corpora (NYT-10k); generalization to other domains not demonstrated.

identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE (in safe and intermediate modes) achieves competitive or higher factual precision than many prior OIE systems (ClausIE, OLLIE, Stanford OIE) on labeled NYT and Wiki test samples, with precision decreasing as modes become more aggressive.
identified_claims.section_anchor: Abstract; Sec. 7.3; Table 4 (NYT and Wiki labeled results)
evidence: Sec. 7.3 Table 4: reported factual precision numbers showing MinIE-S/F/C have higher factual precision than ClausIE and OLLIE in those labeled samples; MinIE-A shows a drop but still often above Stanford OIE.
uncertainty_flags: Labeled samples are small (n≈200 per corpus) and numeric precision values are summarized without confidence intervals or inter-annotator agreement, limiting statistical strength.
Some reported baseline numbers depend on different CoreNLP versions; comparability may be affected.

identified_claims.claim_label: Annotations capture negative/possible facts and attribution
identified_claims.claim_text: Annotations for polarity (negative), modality (possible), and attribution (supplier plus its factuality) allow MinIE to represent information removed during minimization (e.g., negative facts, reported beliefs), addressing issues relevant for downstream reasoning and alleviating absence of negative evidence.
evidence: Introduction: claim that MinIE is first to produce negative-polarity extractions and that annotations help address absence of negative evidence.
Sec. 5 explains how negation words are removed, modality words detected (lexicon from Saurí & Pustejovsky), and attributions detected via dictionary or 'according to' patterns.
uncertainty_flags: Negation/modality/attribution detection limited to lexicon/rule-based 'easy cases'; scope resolution and complex attributions may be missed.
Claim of being 'first' for negative-polarity extractions is asserted without exhaustive comparative evidence in the manuscript.

identified_claims.claim_label: MinIE sometimes reduces extraction count due to deduplication
identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE sometimes produces fewer total extractions than prior systems because prior systems output many redundant extractions; when redundancy is discounted, MinIE is competitive in extraction counts.
evidence: Sec. 7.2 Table 3 shows both total and non-redundant extraction counts; discussion notes Stanford OIE produces many redundant variants and that MinIE sometimes falls behind in raw counts but is competitive when redundancy is removed.
uncertainty_flags: Redundancy is operationalized as 'subsequence' containment; other redundancy definitions could change results.
Non-redundant counts depend on the extraction normalization and are sensitive to exact pre- and post-processing.

identified_claims.claim_text: Main sources of MinIE errors are dependency parsing errors and NER mistakes; collocation/mode errors arise when dictionaries miss true collocations leading to over-minimization.
evidence: Sec. 7.4 explicitly cites dependency parsing and NER errors as main sources and gives examples where missing collocations in D cause incorrect drops.
uncertainty_flags: Relative quantitative contribution of each source to overall errors is not provided; diagnosis is qualitative only.
Error rates may vary with parser/NER versions which are not exhaustively studied.

identified_claims.claim_text: MinIE is implemented on top of ClausIE because ClausIE separates identification of constituents from proposition generation, detects clause types, and is state-of-the-art, enabling MinIE's rewriting pipeline.
evidence: Sec. 3 explains the choice of ClausIE and Sec. 4 describes how MinIE uses and enriches ClausIE output before minimization.
uncertainty_flags: Portability of MinIE to other OIE systems is claimed possible but not empirically evaluated; dependence on ClausIE may transfer its limitations.

strengths.title: Clear, modular pipeline design
strengths.description: The system cleanly separates relation enrichment, basic minimization (polarity/modality/attribution/quantity), and mode-based aggressive minimization, enabling focused analysis and reuse of components.
evidence: Sec. 3 architecture description and Secs. 4–6 detail each component and modes.
Implementation built on ClausIE with explicit enrichment and minimization stages.

strengths.title: Practical implementation and reproducibility intent
strengths.description: Authors implemented MinIE on an existing OIE stack, describe resources used (WordNet/Wiktionary, NYT-built dictionary) and commit to release code, datasets, extractions, and labeling guidelines.
evidence: Sec. 7.1 states all source code, datasets, extractions, labels, and labelling guidelines will be made publically available.
Detailed descriptions of dictionary construction and mode rules in Sec. 6.

strengths.title: Empirical evidence of length reduction and trade-offs
strengths.description: On a large NYT-10k sample, mean extraction lengths decrease monotonically with more aggressive modes, and labeled small-sample evaluation shows a trade-off between aggressiveness and factual precision.
evidence: Table 3 (NYT-10k) shows ClausIE mean 10.9 vs MinIE modes down to 4.7 tokens (MinIE-A).
Table 4 (NYT/Wiki labeled) shows precision drops with aggressiveness but MinIE-S/F/C maintain competitive precision.

concerns.title: Limited coverage and evaluation of factuality detectors
concerns.description: Negation, modality, and attribution detectors are lexicon/rule-based and restricted to 'easy cases'; the manuscript lacks detector-level evaluation (precision/recall) or analysis of missed complex cases (negation scope, embedded modality).
evidence: Sec. 5.1 explicitly uses a tiny negation lexicon {no, not, never, none} and states complex negation is not addressed.
Sec. 5.2/5.3 describe lexicon-based modality and attribution extraction but no detector QA or quantitative coverage is reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide detector-level evaluation on a held-out, annotated subset (measure recall/precision for negation, modality, and attribution detection), report examples of missed scope/complex cases, and quantify how many minimized triples received factuality annotations vs. left unannotated.

concerns.title: Small labeled samples and missing statistical reporting
concerns.description: Factual and attribution precision are reported on small datasets (n≈200 sentences per corpus) without confidence intervals, inter-annotator agreement, or detailed confusion analysis, limiting strength of precision claims.
evidence: Sec. 7.1 describes labeling NYT and Wiki with 200 sentences each; Sec. 7.3 presents precision numbers without CI or IAA.
Prior-stage reviewers flagged absence of IAA and statistical uncertainty.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa or similar), compute and report 95% CIs for precision estimates, increase sample size or run bootstrap resampling, and include per-system numeric precision tables for transparency.

concerns.title: Reliance on single upstream pipeline and limited robustness analysis
concerns.description: MinIE depends on ClausIE and a specific CoreNLP version (3.5.1) for parsing and NER; the paper identifies parser/NER as primary error sources but does not test portability or sensitivity to alternative parsers/NERs.
evidence: Sec. 3 and 7.1 state MinIE implemented on ClausIE adapted to CoreNLP 3.5.1; Sec. 7.4 points to parser/NER errors as main sources.
Shared analysis notes architecture ties results to upstream components.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run an ablation/re-sensitivity analysis using at least one alternative dependency parser/NER configuration (e.g., newer CoreNLP or spaCy) and report how many minimizations or annotation changes occur; quantify error transfer.

concerns.title: Dictionary D underspecified and domain sensitivity untested
concerns.description: MinIE-F/C rely on dictionary D (WordNet/Wiktionary or corpus frequency ≥10); construction details and domain-generalizability are under-specified and no sensitivity analysis is provided to show impact on over-/under-minimization.
evidence: Sec. 6.2 describes using multi-word expressions from WordNet/Wiktionary for MinIE-C and building D from NYT corpus frequency ≥10 for MinIE-F; choices not fully enumerated.
Sec. 7.4 gives examples where missing collocations in D cause errors.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide exact dictionary statistics (size, examples), perform ablation varying frequency threshold and D sources, and report resulting precision/minimality trade-offs across domains (NYT vs Wiki).

concerns.title: Using mean token length as sole proxy for minimality
concerns.description: The paper uses mean extraction length and stddev as the primary minimality metric but does not measure semantic preservation or downstream utility; shorter triples may lose necessary context despite annotations.
evidence: Sec. 7.1 explicitly states mean word count and stddev used as proxy for minimality.
Shared analysis notes no downstream task evaluation or human utility judgments.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add human evaluation of semantic adequacy (judges rate whether minimized triple+annotations preserve essential meaning), or evaluate on a downstream task (simple QA or KB population) measuring practical utility.

concerns.title: Operational redundancy definition may bias recall comparisons
concerns.description: Redundancy is defined as subsequence containment which may conflate semantically distinct but lexically overlapping extractions or miss other redundancy types; reported 'non-redundant' counts may depend heavily on this choice.
evidence: Sec. 7.1 defines redundant triple t1 if subsequence of another t2 from same sentence; Sec. 7.2 uses this to compute non-redundant counts.
Discussion notes Stanford OIE produces many shorter redundant variants.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report alternative redundancy measures (e.g., normalized lexical forms, argument normalization, or semantic equivalence heuristics) and show how sensitive non-redundant counts are to the redundancy definition.

comparable_works.relevance: Base system used for MinIE implementation and comparison baseline.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: ClausIE provides clause decomposition and proposition generation; MinIE builds on it for rewriting and adds annotations and mode-based minimization.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 3, Sec. 4

comparable_works.relevance: Introduced annotated OIE extractions (attribution and clause modifiers); prior art in using annotations.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE adopts attribution-style annotations and extends to polarity/modality/quantity annotations; OLLIE limited to ccomp patterns.
comparable_works.source_trace: Introduction; Sec. 2 Related Work

comparable_works.relevance: Closest in spirit regarding aggressive minimization; used as baseline.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both perform aggressive deletion based on dependency types; MinIE differs by externalizing factuality and by finer-grained modes and dictionary-based stabilization.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 2 Related Work; Sec. 7.3 comparisons

comparable_works.relevance: Introduced frequency-based lexical constraints to avoid overly-specific relations; inspires MinIE-F frequency mode.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: MinIE generalizes frequency idea to subjects and arguments and uses multi-mode minimization.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sec. 2 Related Work; Sec. 6.2

uncertainty_flags: Factuality (polarity/modality) and attribution detectors are lexicon/rule-based and limited to 'easy cases'; coverage of complex linguistic phenomena (negation scope, nested modality) is untested.
Precision estimates rely on small labeled samples (NYT n=200, Wiki n=200) without confidence intervals or inter-annotator agreement.
Dictionary D construction choices (WordNet/Wiktionary vs corpus frequency) are under-specified; domain dependence and sensitivity not analyzed.
Dependence on ClausIE and Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1 means reported results are tied to those upstream tools; portability is untested.
Mean token count is a coarse proxy for minimality and may not reflect semantic adequacy or downstream task utility.
alternative_interpretations: Shorter average extraction length may reflect deletion of words that downstream tasks actually need; higher precision on small samples might be due to removal of noisy, long relations rather than true preservation of informative content.

MinIE's gains in precision could stem partly from producing fewer (and thus more selective) extractions; the apparent competitiveness in recall after de-duplication may mask loss of distinct but detailed facts.
Good performance in NYT-10k and NYT-labeled may be partly corpus-specific because MinIE-F is built from the NYT corpus; performance could degrade on other genres.
transparency_notes: Authors commit to releasing code, datasets, extractions, labels, and labeling guidelines which is crucial for auditing detector-level performance and reproducing dictionary D construction.
Exact contents and size of dictionary D (WordNet/Wiktionary subsets and NYT frequency cutoff results) are not listed in the manuscript; release should include these artifacts.
Labeling protocol mentions factuality-aware entailment decisions; detailed labeling guidelines and IAA metrics are necessary to interpret precision results.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While MinIE's idea of minimizing extractions and recording removed semantics has antecedents (OLLIE, Stanford OIE, ReVerb), the specific combination of polarity/modality/attribution/quantity annotations together with multi-mode, dictionary-guided minimization is not a trivial replication; novelty must be separated from empirical validity which depends on detector coverage and evaluation robustness.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If factuality and attribution detectors achieve high recall/precision (beyond 'easy cases'), minimized triples plus annotations will preserve usable semantics for downstream tasks.
If dictionary D is constructed with comprehensive, domain-relevant collocations or learned robustly from diverse corpora, MinIE-F/C modes will avoid over-minimization across genres.
If MinIE is robust to parser/NER variability (i.e., similar outputs across parsers), it can be ported widely and serve as a practical rewriting layer.

novelty_lenses.rationale: MinIE integrates known techniques (relation enrichment, lexicon-based factuality detection, dictionary-guided collocation retention) into a cohesive pipeline and extends annotations to polarity/modality/quantity beyond prior OIE systems. This is an incremental but practically useful advance.
evidence: Sec. 2 situates MinIE relative to OLLIE and Stanford OIE and claims additional/finer-grained annotations and modes.
Combination of annotation types + mode control is not present in a single prior system in the manuscript.
uncertainty_flags: Degree of novelty depends on whether annotation coverage and minimization modes empirically outperform or provide distinct downstream utility beyond previous methods; this is currently under-evidenced.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Methodological contributions (modes, dictionary use, annotation schema) are promising but need further validation: detector-level metrics, parser/NER sensitivity, and evaluation on downstream tasks to establish real-world impact.
evidence: Secs. 5–6 describe algorithms and resources but lack quantitative detector evaluations and robustness tests.
Sec. 7 evaluation focuses on mean length and small-sample precision; downstream effects not tested.
uncertainty_flags: Without detector-level and downstream evaluations, methodological novelty remains provisional as practical usefulness is uncertain.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident in claims directly supported by manuscript evidence (e.g., implementation exists, mean length reductions on NYT-10k, presence of annotation types). Confidence is lower for broader claims about generalizable precision/utility because labeled sample sizes are small, detector coverage is limited to easy cases, and robustness to upstream tools and domain shifts is untested.

consensus_findings: MinIE is a concrete, implemented rewriting layer built on ClausIE that (a) enriches ClausIE relations, (b) removes certain lexical material (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) and records them as annotations, and (c) offers multiple minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) that trade off minimality and precision.
All reviewers observe that MinIE yields substantially shorter surface extractions (mean token length decreases monotonically with aggressiveness) on the reported NYT-10k corpus.
Reviewers agree that MinIE's factuality/modality/attribution detectors are rule/lexicon-based and deliberately focused on 'easy cases', i.e., coverage is limited.

There is agreement that upstream components (ClausIE, dependency parser, NER / Stanford CoreNLP) substantially influence MinIE's outputs and that parser/NER errors are a primary source of MinIE errors.

All reviewers note the construction and role of the dictionary D (for frequency/collocations modes) is important and under-specified in the manuscript, and that D's domain dependence can affect minimization behavior.

The labeled evaluation used for precision (NYT and Wiki, ~200 sentences each) is judged too small by reviewers for strong statistical generalization; inter-annotator agreement and confidence intervals are missing.
There is consensus that mean token count (µ ± σ) is a coarse proxy for minimality and does not by itself prove semantic adequacy or downstream utility of minimized triples.

Reviewers uniformly recommend additional validation experiments (detector-level evaluation, parser/NER sensitivity, dictionary sensitivity, expanded labeling with IAA, downstream-task evaluation) to strengthen empirical claims.
disagreements: Degree of novelty / impact: some reviewers characterize MinIE as a useful incremental engineering contribution (integration of known components), while at least one reviewer views the representation change (minimize surface triples + explicit factual annotations) as conceptually novel and potentially disruptive. The authors' claims about being 'first' to emit negative-polarity extractions are also questioned (asserted but not exhaustively evidenced).

Strength and generalizability of precision claims: reviewers differ on how convincing the reported precision numbers are. Some accept that MinIE-S/F/C are competitive within the evaluated setting (with caveats), whereas others emphasize that small labeled samples, missing statistical reporting, and upstream-tool differences make the precision comparisons provisional.

Portability claims: reviewers disagree on how plausible it is that MinIE's techniques 'can be integrated into any OIE system' without adaptation. Some treat portability as plausible in principle but untested; others flag this as an important unvalidated assumption that could materially affect outcomes.
uncertainty_hotspots: Factuality/modality/attribution detectors: limited lexicon/rule coverage (negation lexicon limited to a few tokens; modality based on simplified lexicons) creates uncertainty about detection recall and false negatives/positives, and about annotation correctness in non-‘easy’ constructions (negation scope, nested modalities, indirect attributions).

Dictionary D construction and domain sensitivity: how D was built (exact WordNet/Wiktionary subsets, corpus frequency thresholds, whether evaluation data were excluded) is insufficiently reported; this affects MinIE-F/C behaviors and risks over- or under-minimization in other domains.

Upstream-tool sensitivity: MinIE's reliance on ClausIE plus a specific parser/NER configuration (Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1) means reported results may change with parser/NER versions or alternative OIE base systems; the magnitude and direction of these changes are unknown.

Evaluation reliability: small labeled samples (~200 sentences per corpus), absent inter-annotator agreement, and missing confidence intervals undermine certainty of factual and attribution precision estimates.

Minimality vs informativeness: token-count reductions are clear, but it is uncertain to what extent annotations plus minimized triples preserve the semantics required by realistic downstream tasks (KB population, QA, inference).
Redundancy operationalization: the subsequence-based redundancy definition is an operational choice; its sensitivity and potential biases versus semantic equivalence measures are not quantified.
model_diversity_effects: Structure-analyst lens emphasized logical coherence, chaining of assumptions, and detection of weak links (focused criticism: lexicon limits, mean-length proxy). This contributed to strong calls for detector audits and downstream validation.

Methodology/reproducibility lens prioritized experiments, artifact disclosure, and statistical reporting; reviewers with this role drove demands for IAA, confidence intervals, full numeric tables, and scripts to build dictionary D.

Novelty-focused reviewers split: incremental-assessors highlighted integration and engineering value; disruptive-thinkers flagged conceptual novelty (surface minimality + factual annotations) and were more willing to treat the idea as an innovation signal despite practical limitations. This diversity produced controlled disagreement about the significance of the contribution.

Claim-verifier reviewers stressed evidence-grounded claims and drew attention to empirical traceability (which numbers are fully reported, which are only summarized), reinforcing requests for full result tables and detector-level metrics.

Net effect: role diversity produced complementary critiques (architectural, empirical, and conceptual). No single perspective dominated; together they expose both consistent strengths (clear pipeline, measurable length reduction, useful annotation idea) and systematic gaps (detector validation, reproducibility artifacts, statistical rigor).
meta_review.editor_guidance: As central decision-maker, consider the following prioritized requests to the authors before making a final judgment: (1) Provide and release the full artifacts required for reproducibility: codebase, exact dictionaries (D), lexicons for negation/modality/attribution, scripts to build D, full ClausIE adaptation details, and parser/NER configuration. (2) Add detector-level evaluations: create a gold annotated subset for polarity, modality, and attribution detection and report precision/recall/F1; show propagation effects on triple-level factual precision. (3) Strengthen labeled evaluation: increase labeled sample sizes or provide bootstrap confidence intervals; report inter-annotator agreement and make labeling guidelines and raw labels available. (4) Perform robustness/ablation experiments: re-run MinIE with at least one alternative parser/NER and (if feasible) on ClausIE outputs produced with different CoreNLP versions or another base OIE system to show portability/ sensitivity. (5) Provide dictionary-sensitivity analyses: report D size, examples, and ablations over frequency thresholds and cross-corpus D construction (e.g., build D on different corpora and test transfer). (6) Complement token-count minimality metrics with semantic adequacy evidence: human judgments of semantic preservation for minimized+annotated triples and/or an extrinsic downstream task (simple KB population or QA) demonstrating practical utility. (7) Clarify or temper claims about novelty (e.g., 'first' negative-polarity extractions) unless exhaustive prior-art checks are provided. These additions will reduce epistemic uncertainty, enable reproducibility, and contextualize contributions for the community.
meta_review.author_guidance: To address reviewers' concerns and improve evidential support, please provide the following actionable items: (A) Release all code, configuration files, exact lexicon lists (negation, modality, attribution), dictionary D contents or scripts to build it, and exact ClausIE/CoreNLP versions and parameters used. (B) Create and publish a small gold corpus with fine-grained annotations for polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities; report detector-level precision/recall and examples of typical failures (negation scope, nested modality). (C) Expand or resample the labeled precision evaluation (NYT/Wiki) to increase sample sizes or provide bootstrap-derived 95% confidence intervals; supply inter-annotator agreement statistics and labeling guidelines. (D) Run sensitivity experiments: (1) swap the dependency parser/NER for at least one alternative (newer CoreNLP or spaCy) and report changes in extraction length and precision; (2) evaluate MinIE variants when applied to outputs of at least one other OIE extractor if feasible. (E) Publish full numeric result tables (per-system per-metric) rather than summarized parentheses to enable auditing. (F) Report dictionary D construction details (sources, thresholds, number of multi-word expressions, examples) and a threshold-sensitivity ablation (e.g., frequency cutoffs 5/10/20). (G) Add intrinsic semantic-evaluation: human judgments (Does minimized triple + annotations preserve the sentence-level fact?) and/or a lightweight extrinsic evaluation (e.g., simple KB population or fact-checking downstream task) to demonstrate preserved utility. (H) Revise overstated claims (e.g., 'first' negative-polarity extractions) unless you provide comprehensive prior-art evidence. Implementing these actions will materially reduce reviewer uncertainties and make claims more empirically grounded.
transparency_report: Missing or insufficiently specified artifacts: exact dictionary D contents and construction scripts (for MinIE-F and MinIE-C), full lexicon lists used for negation/modality/attribution, and the exact ClausIE adaptation/parameters and parser/NER configuration (Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1 note is insufficient alone).

Evaluation reporting gaps: labeled datasets (raw labels), labeling guidelines, inter-annotator agreement statistics, and full per-system numeric precision/recall tables with confidence intervals are not included in the manuscript materials provided to reviewers.

Reproducibility aids requested: scripts to replicate extraction statistics on NYT-10k, seed values or deterministic settings if applicable, and instructions for reconstructing the frequency-based dictionary D without leaking evaluation data.

Error analysis currently qualitative: reviewers request quantitative breakdowns attributing errors to parser/NER vs dictionary misses vs minimizer logic, ideally via an error taxonomy and sampled confusion matrices.
epistemic_limits: This synthesis is constrained to the manuscript excerpts and the specialist reviewer reports provided. I did not inspect the authors' code, dictionaries, or raw labels and cannot independently verify empirical numbers beyond the reported tables and reviewer summaries. The assessment relies on reviewers' interpretations and reported evidence; any unreported experiments, additional artifacts, or later clarifications from the authors could materially change the balance of evidence. Prior-art exhaustiveness (e.g., claims of being the 'first' to output negative-polarity extractions) cannot be adjudicated here without a dedicated literature search beyond the supplied references. Finally, quantitative judgments about generalizability and downstream impact are limited by the absence of detector-level metrics, alternative-parser ablations, and downstream-task evaluations in the materials reviewed.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript presents MinIE, a rewriting layer on top of ClausIE that (1) enriches ClausIE relations, (2) removes certain lexical material (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities) and records it as structured annotations, and (3) applies configurable minimization modes (Safe, Frequency, Collocations, Aggressive) to produce shorter OIE extractions. Empirical evidence shows consistent reductions in mean extraction length on an NYT-10k corpus and that conservative/intermediate modes often retain competitive factual and attribution precision on two labeled 200-sentence samples. Core uncertainties arise from lexicon/rule-based detectors limited to 'easy cases', dependence on a specific upstream pipeline (ClausIE + Stanford CoreNLP), underspecified dictionary construction, and small labeled evaluation samples without reported inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals.
strengths: Clear, modular pipeline (relation enrichment → basic minimization with factuality/quantity/attribution annotations → mode-based minimization) that is implementable and interpretable.
Practical implementation integrated with ClausIE and promise to release code/data, enabling reproducibility if artifacts are published.
Demonstrated, sizable reduction in surface extraction length (NYT-10k µ/σ) with an explicit precision/minimality trade-off across modes.
Brings factuality (polarity, modality), attribution and quantity annotations into OIE outputs—an important representation advance for downstream reasoning.
limitations: Factuality/modality/attribution detectors are lexicon/rule-based and restricted to 'easy cases' (e.g., small negation lexicon, simplified modality lexicons); no detector-level precision/recall is reported, leaving unclear how often annotations are correct or missed on complex linguistic phenomena (negation scope, nested modality, indirect attributions).

Labeled evaluation for factual and attribution precision uses small samples (NYT n=200, Wiki n=200) without inter-annotator agreement, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; this limits strength and generalizability of precision claims.

Dictionary D (for MinIE-F and MinIE-C) is underspecified: exact contents, size, construction scripts, frequency thresholds and whether evaluation data were excluded are not provided; this creates domain-dependence and risk of overfitting (e.g., building D on the same corpus used in evaluation).

Heavy reliance on a single upstream stack (ClausIE + Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1 and an NER) is acknowledged as an error source, but portability/sensitivity to alternative parsers, NERs or base OIE systems is not empirically evaluated.
open_questions: Please provide detector-level evaluation: on a gold-annotated subset, what are precision/recall/F1 for negation, modality (CT/PS), attribution detection, and quantity normalization? Provide representative failure examples (e.g., negation scope misses).

How exactly was the dictionary D constructed for MinIE-F and MinIE-C (sources, number of entries, threshold choices)? Were evaluation sentences excluded when building D? Provide scripts or dump of D or clear reproduction instructions.

Provide inter-annotator agreement statistics and confidence intervals for the labeled NYT/Wiki precision evaluations; if sample sizes are limited, can you expand labeled sets or provide bootstrap CIs to quantify uncertainty?

How sensitive are MinIE outputs to upstream components? Report ablations re-running MinIE with an alternative parser/NER (or ClausIE reconfigured) and quantify changes in minimization decisions, annotations, and precision/length metrics.
consensus_snapshot: MinIE is a coherent, implemented rewriting pipeline that reduces surface extraction length substantially and formalizes factuality/attribution/quantity annotations.
Conservative/intermediate minimization modes provide a controllable precision/minimality trade-off; aggressive mode is shortest but risks precision loss.

Key methodological weak points are lexicon/rule detectors with limited coverage, underspecified dictionary construction, dependence on upstream parsing/NER, and small labeled-sample statistical reporting.
disagreement_snapshot: Assessors disagree on the degree of novelty/impact: some view MinIE as a meaningful incremental engineering contribution (integration and practical modes), while others see the representation idea (minimizing surface triples + externalized factual annotations) as conceptually novel and potentially disruptive. The manuscript does not fully resolve whether this representation change yields broader downstream benefits.

There is variation in how persuasive the precision comparisons are: some reviewers accept competitive precision within the reported setting (with caveats), while others consider the small labeled samples and upstream-tool differences sufficient to treat precision claims as provisional.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty about annotation correctness and coverage for complex factual phenomena (negation scope, nested modalities) due to lexicon/rule detectors and missing detector-level metrics.
Uncertainty about generalization across domains because dictionary D construction and thresholds are not fully specified and may be NYT-dependent.
Uncertainty about robustness to different parsers/NERs or base OIE systems because only one toolchain (ClausIE + CoreNLP 3.5.1) was used and no portability ablations are reported.
Uncertainty about practical benefit for downstream tasks because minimality is evaluated primarily by token counts rather than semantic adequacy or downstream utility.
source_trace: ClausIE (Del Corro & Gemulla, 2013) — used as MinIE substrate and baseline; manuscript Sec.3-4 describe integration with ClausIE.
Stanford OIE (Angeli et al., 2015) — baseline for aggressive minimization comparisons; referenced in Sec.2 and Sec.7 comparisons.
OLLIE (Schmitz et al., 2012) — prior annotated OIE system (attribution) cited in Related Work and Sec.5 for annotation lineage.
ReVerb (Fader et al., 2011) — frequency-based lexical constraint inspiration for MinIE-F; discussed in Sec.2 and Sec.6.2.
Saurí & Pustejovsky (2012) — factuality taxonomy (CT/PS) adopted conceptually for modality/polarity annotations; cited in Sec.5.
Stanford CoreNLP 3.5.1 — parser/NER tool referenced as upstream pipeline; Sec.7.4 and shared analyses identify parser/NER errors as main error sources.
transparency_notes: Authors state an intent to release code, datasets, extractions, labels and labelling guidelines; reviewers flagged that reproducibility requires also releasing the exact dictionaries (D), lexicon lists used for negation/modality/attribution, ClausIE/CoreNLP adaptation scripts and parameter settings, and raw labeled data with annotator IDs and guidelines. Missing these artifacts prevents full audit of detector performance, dictionary construction, and statistical claims.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request a revision that prioritizes reproducibility and empirical robustness: (1) publish code, parser/NER/ClausIE configurations, lexicons, and dictionary D or build scripts; (2) add detector-level evaluation (gold annotations for polarity/modality/attribution/quantities) with precision/recall; (3) expand or statistically qualify labeled precision results with inter-annotator agreement and confidence intervals or significance tests; (4) run sensitivity/portability ablations (alternative parser/NER and, if feasible, another base extractor) and a dictionary-threshold sensitivity analysis; (5) complement token-count minimality with human semantic-preservation judgments or a simple downstream task evaluation. These items materially reduce epistemic uncertainty and are necessary to validate generality claims.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript, please (A) release all artifacts needed for replication: code, exact lexicons, dictionary D (or scripts and corpus seeds to rebuild it), ClausIE/CoreNLP configuration details; (B) annotate and publish a gold set for factuality/attribution detection and report detector-level metrics and qualitative failure modes (negation scope, nested modality); (C) provide inter-annotator agreement and confidence intervals for labeled precision results or expand labeled sets and re-report metrics with statistical tests; (D) run ablations substituting alternative parsers/NERs and report changes in annotations/minimizations and precision/length metrics; (E) give full numeric per-system tables (not only summaries) and a sensitivity analysis for dictionary thresholds and redundancy definitions; (F) include human judgments or a downstream-task evaluation to validate that minimized+annotated triples preserve usable semantics. Also temper any strong 'first' novelty claims unless comprehensive literature checks are supplied.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: MinIE is a well-specified rewriting layer that minimizes OIE extractions while exporting removed semantics as annotations (polarity, modality, attribution, quantities). The system is implemented on ClausIE and exposes conservative-to-aggressive modes that trade precision for brevity. Empirically, MinIE shortens extractions substantially on NYT-10k and conservative/intermediate modes often maintain competitive precision on two labeled small samples.

Strengths: Clear modular pipeline; implemented system with modes and planned artifact release; measurable reductions in token-length; explicit factuality/attribution/quantity annotations address a practical OIE representation gap.

Limitations: (1) Annotation detectors are rule/lexicon-based and limited to 'easy cases' with no detector-level metrics, risking missed or incorrect annotations in complex constructions (negation scope, nested modality). (2) Labeled precision evaluation is small (n≈200 per corpus) without reported inter-annotator agreement or confidence intervals, weakening claims of competitive precision. (3) Dictionary D construction is under-documented (sources, thresholds, size) and may be domain-specific or overfit to NYT. (4) Dependence on a single upstream toolchain (ClausIE + CoreNLP 3.5.1) is not accompanied by portability/sensitivity analyses.

Open Questions: (1) Provide detector-level precision/recall for polarity/modality/attribution and examples of systematic failures (e.g., negation scope). (2) Publish the exact dictionary D (or scripts to build it) and state whether evaluation splits were excluded from D construction. (3) Report inter-annotator agreement and confidence intervals for labeled precision results or enlarge labeled samples. (4) Show robustness by re-running MinIE with an alternative parser/NER (and if possible, on another base OIE system) and report changes.

Transparency: Reviewers request full artifact release: code, lexicons, dictionary D contents/scripts, ClausIE/CoreNLP configs, labeling guidelines, raw labels and annotator IDs, and full numeric result tables with CIs. Without these artifacts, many empirical claims remain hard to audit.

Epistemic limits: This synthesis relies on the manuscript excerpts and specialist reviews; I did not access the authors' code, dictionaries, or raw labels. Some claims (e.g., 'first' to emit negative-polarity extractions) cannot be validated here without a broader literature search. The reviewers' judgments were consistent on core strengths and gaps but differ on novelty and generalization significance.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have moderate-to-high confidence that MinIE, as described, is implemented and produces the reported token-length reductions on the supplied NYT-10k corpus (strong internal evidence). Confidence is lower for broader claims about generalizable precision, annotation coverage, and downstream utility because of small labeled samples, lexicon/rule detector limits, underspecified dictionary construction, and lack of robustness ablations; these factors justify a conservative lower bound and a cautious upper bound.
